anchor_quote:
The improper integral at zero is finite because
\(x\log x\to0\) as \(x\downarrow0\).
text:
The width of this interval,
\[
 (n+1)\log(n+1)-n\log n=\log(n+1)+n\log(1+1/n),
\]
exceeds \(\log(n+1)\) and so grows without bound. Feller reads the double
inequality as a hint to compare \(\log n!\) with some quantity near the
arithmetic mean of its two outer members, and takes
\((n+\tfrac12)\log n-n\) as the simplest such quantity; that is why the
difference \(d_n\) below is the object estimated
\cite[II.9, pp.~52--53]{Feller1968ProbabilityI}. The quantity is near the
mean in a precise sense. For \(t>0\),
\(\log(1+t)=\int_0^t(1+v)^{-1}dv\) has its integrand strictly between
\((1+t)^{-1}\) and one, so \(t/(1+t)<\log(1+t)<t\). The arithmetic mean of
the outer members is
\(m_n=\tfrac12\{n\log n+(n+1)\log(n+1)\}-n\), and
\[
 m_n-\bigl\{(n+\tfrac12)\log n-n\bigr\}=\tfrac12(n+1)\log(1+1/n).
\]
With \(t=1/n\) the right side lies strictly between \(\tfrac12\) and
\(\tfrac12(1+1/n)\leq1\). Thus the comparison quantity stays within
distance one of the midpoint of an interval whose width tends to infinity.

anchor_quote:
We now discharge the constant referral by Feller's
probability-mass argument. This argument does not use a
previously established normal limit.
text:
We now determine the constant. Feller proves \(e^C=\sqrt{2\pi}\) only in
VII.2. He states that this proof is elementary and does not depend on the
material of his chapters IV--VI, and that he defers it to chapter VII
because of its natural connection with the normal approximation theorem
\cite[II.9, p.~53]{Feller1968ProbabilityI}. The determination itself is his
note on the constant in VII.2 \cite[VII.2, p.~180, n.~3]{Feller1968ProbabilityI}.
It replaces \(\pi\) in the central-term approximation (2.6) by an unknown
constant and compares the probability of the interval from the centre to
\(z_2\) standard units, bounded by means of the tail estimate
VI,(3.5), with the Gaussian tail bounds VII,(1.8). The tail estimate is
proved directly in \cref{thm:p15-stirling-tail-premises} from the ratio of
consecutive binomial masses and a geometric series, and the Gaussian bounds
are proved there by differentiation. The argument below therefore uses only
those two elementary comparisons and the logarithmic estimates of
\cref{thm:p15-stirling-log-tools}; in particular it does not use a
previously established normal limit.

Fix \(0<M<\infty\). For \(k\leq M\sqrt n\), the logarithmic
error bound gives
\[
 \log\frac{p_n(k)}{p_n(0)}
    =-\frac{k^2}{n}+E_{n,k},\qquad
 |E_{n,k}|\leq\frac2{n^2}\sum_{j=1}^k j^2
                         \longrightarrow0
\]
uniformly in that range. Symmetry handles negative \(k\).
This is the central-ratio argument in the cited VII.2
passage with the constant still undetermined.
With \(h_n=2/\sqrt{2n}\) it gives, uniformly on every
bounded interval of \(x=k h_n\),
\[
 \frac{p_n(k)}{h_n}\longrightarrow A^{-1}e^{-x^2/2}
                  =c\phi(x),\qquad c=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}A.
\]
Here the uniform limit notation means that the supremum
of the difference over the indicated lattice points tends
to zero.
text:
Let \(K_n>0\) satisfy \(K_n^3/n^2\to0\). This is Feller's range
condition (2.4); his \(a_k\), \(\nu\) and \(K_\nu\) are \(p_n(k)\), \(n\)
and \(K_n\) here, and his number of trials \(2\nu\) is \(2n\)
\cite[VII.2, pp.~179--180]{Feller1968ProbabilityI}. We first show that,
for all \(n\geq1\) and all integers \(0\leq k\leq n/2\),
\[
 \log\frac{p_n(k)}{p_n(0)}=-\frac{k^2}{n}+E_{n,k},\qquad
 |E_{n,k}|\leq\frac{k^3}{n^2}.
\]
For \(k=0\) take \(E_{n,0}=0\). For \(k\geq1\), divide numerator and
denominator of the exact ratio by \(n^k\):
\[
 \frac{p_n(k)}{p_n(0)}
   =\prod_{j=1}^{k}\Bigl(1-\frac{j-1}n\Bigr)
     \Bigm/\prod_{j=1}^{k}\Bigl(1+\frac jn\Bigr).
\]
Each \(t\) among \(-(j-1)/n\) and \(j/n\), \(1\leq j\leq k\), satisfies
\(|t|\leq k/n\leq1/2\), so the first estimate of
\cref{thm:p15-stirling-log-tools} replaces \(\log(1+t)\) by \(t\) with an
error of at most \(t^2\). The retained terms sum exactly to
\[
 -\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^{k}(j-1)-\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^{k}j
   =-\frac{k(k-1)+k(k+1)}{2n}=-\frac{k^2}n,
\]
and the errors add to at most
\[
 \frac1{n^2}\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}j^2+\sum_{j=1}^{k}j^2\Bigr)
   =\frac{2k^3+k}{3n^2}\leq\frac{k^3}{n^2},
\]
since \(k\leq k^3\). Eventually \(K_n^3/n^2\leq1/8\), and then
\(K_n=(K_n^3/n^2)^{1/3}n^{2/3}\leq n^{2/3}/2\leq n/2\). Hence
\[
 \sup_{0\leq k<K_n}|E_{n,k}|\leq\frac{K_n^3}{n^2}\longrightarrow0 .
\]
This is Feller's (2.5), \(p_n(k)\sim p_n(0)e^{-k^2/n}\), with his error
bound \(k^3/n^2\), uniformly over the whole range \(0\leq k<K_n\)
\cite[VII.2, p.~180]{Feller1968ProbabilityI}. Since
\(p_n(-k)=p_n(k)\), it holds uniformly over \(|k|<K_n\).
Put \(h_n=2/\sqrt{2n}=\sqrt{2/n}\), so that
\(h_n\phi(kh_n)=(\pi n)^{-1/2}e^{-k^2/n}\), and \(c=\sqrt{2\pi}/A\).
The unknown-\(A\) form of the central term then gives, for \(|k|<K_n\)
and all large \(n\),
\[
 \frac{p_n(k)}{c\,h_n\phi(kh_n)}=e^{E_{n,|k|}+r_{2n}-2r_n},
\]
and the right side tends to one uniformly in that range, because
\(r_n\to0\). Once \(A=\sqrt{2\pi}\) is proved below, \(c=1\) and this is
Feller's basic relation (2.7), \(p_n(k)\sim h_n\phi(kh_n)\), valid
whenever \(k\) is restricted to a range \(|k|<K_n\) satisfying (2.4)
\cite[VII.2, pp.~180--181]{Feller1968ProbabilityI}. Feller uses it mainly
for \(k\) of the order of \(\sqrt n\), where (2.4) holds trivially, and
the determination of the constant needs only that case.

Fix \(0<M<\infty\) and take \(K_n=M\sqrt n+1\), so that
\(K_n^3/n^2\to0\). With \(x=kh_n\), every lattice point with
\(|x|\leq M\) has \(|k|\leq M\sqrt{n/2}<K_n\), and
\begin{align*}
 \Bigl|\frac{p_n(k)}{h_n}-A^{-1}e^{-x^2/2}\Bigr|
   &=A^{-1}e^{-x^2/2}\bigl|e^{E_{n,|k|}+r_{2n}-2r_n}-1\bigr|\\
   &\leq A^{-1}\sup_{|j|<K_n}\bigl|e^{E_{n,|j|}+r_{2n}-2r_n}-1\bigr|.
\end{align*}
Hence, uniformly on every bounded interval of \(x=kh_n\),
\[
 \frac{p_n(k)}{h_n}\longrightarrow A^{-1}e^{-x^2/2}
                  =c\phi(x).
\]
Here the uniform limit notation means that the supremum
of the difference over the indicated lattice points tends
to zero.

anchor_quote:
The proof first obtains a finite logarithmic constant, then
determines it by Feller's probability-mass argument without
assuming a normal-limit theorem. It also supplies an independent
determination using the already proved cosine-integral central
coefficient.
text:
The proof follows Feller's II.9. The elementary bounds
\(n\log n-n<\log n!<(n+1)\log(n+1)-n\) suggest comparing \(\log n!\) with
a quantity near the arithmetic mean of the two outer members; the
simplest is \((n+\tfrac12)\log n-n\), and estimating the difference yields
a finite logarithmic constant \(C\) \cite[pp.~52--53]{Feller1968ProbabilityI}.
Feller states that the proof of \(e^C=\sqrt{2\pi}\) is elementary and
does not depend on his chapters IV--VI, and places it in VII.2 because of
its natural connection with the normal approximation theorem
\cite[p.~53]{Feller1968ProbabilityI}. The proof carries out that
determination without assuming a normal-limit theorem. On the way it
proves Feller's central-ratio approximations (2.5) and (2.7) in their full
range: if \(K_n>0\) and \(K_n^3/n^2\to0\), then uniformly in integers
\(|k|<K_n\)
\[
 \frac{4^{-n}\binom{2n}{n+k}}{4^{-n}\binom{2n}{n}e^{-k^2/n}}\longrightarrow1,
 \qquad
 \frac{4^{-n}\binom{2n}{n+k}}{\sqrt{2/n}\,\phi\bigl(k\sqrt{2/n}\bigr)}
 \longrightarrow1,
\]
and the logarithm of the first ratio is at most \(|k|^3/n^2\) in absolute
value whenever \(|k|\leq n/2\) \cite[VII.2, pp.~180--181]{Feller1968ProbabilityI}.
It also supplies an independent determination of the constant using the
already proved cosine-integral central coefficient.

text:
Feller weighs the first two assertions against each other. He grants that
the difference of the two sides of Stirling's formula grows beyond every
bound, and judges that ``it is the percentage error which really
matters''; that error decreases steadily, and he finds the approximation
remarkably accurate even for small \(n\)
\cite[II.9, p.~52]{Feller1968ProbabilityI}. Every approximation that this
chapter derives from the formula is of the relative kind. The local theorem
\cref{thm:p15-stirling-local-rademacher} and the constant determination
compare probabilities with their approximations through ratios, and the
two rate theorems take logarithms divided by a multiple of \(n\); in each, Stirling's
formula enters only through \(n!/A_n=e^{r_n}\), whose logarithm is below
\(1/(12n)\).
